title: Tickle v. Barton (1956)
summary: A plea alleging that deception induced an out-of-state defendant to enter the forum stated a basis for challenging service.
notes:
Keep this West Virginia service doctrine distinct from the constitutional minimum-contacts inquiry and from immunity for witnesses attending court.

Rule stated by the court: when a nonresident is "inveigled, enticed or induced, by fraud, trickery, artifice or wrongful device for which a party is responsible by virtue of the action of his attorney to come within the jurisdiction for the purpose of enabling such party to obtain personal service of process, service of process which results from such fraud, trickery, artifice or wrongful device is invalid and does not justify the exercise of jurisdiction by such court over the person so served with process."

Richard Tickle, a minor, sued Raymond Barton, a resident of Austinville, Virginia, in the Circuit Court of McDowell County for injuries inflicted by a motor vehicle on private property; Barton alleged that Tickle's attorney telephoned him and refused to identify himself when asked, while persuading him to attend a banquet in West Virginia.

sections.Parties: Tickle, an injured minor, sued Barton and Coleman. Barton was a Virginia resident. The service dispute concerned alleged conduct by the plaintiff’s lawyer directed at bringing Barton into West Virginia.
sections.Material Facts: After an earlier effort to obtain jurisdiction under the motorist procedure, the plaintiff’s lawyer allegedly induced Barton to attend a football banquet in West Virginia. Barton’s plea claimed that the lawyer concealed his identity and used a false account of his authority and the invitation to secure Barton’s attendance. Barton was then served while present in the state. The banquet’s existence did not by itself answer whether deception had procured his presence.
sections.Procedural History: Barton challenged the summons through a plea in abatement. The plaintiff demurred to that plea, arguing that even the alleged facts did not justify relief. The trial court overruled the demurrer and certified the legal question. The West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals upheld that ruling. Because the issue arose on demurrer, the court evaluated the sufficiency of the allegations rather than deciding their truth after a trial.
sections.Issue: Do allegations that the plaintiff’s lawyer deceptively induced a nonresident to enter the state provide a legally sufficient objection to the resulting service?
sections.Holding: Yes. The allegations, taken as true at this stage, described fraud in procuring the defendant’s presence and therefore stated a sufficient plea against service.
sections.Reasoning: Judicial process depends on legitimate means of bringing defendants before the court. The court would not allow the party invoking its authority to obtain the geographic predicate for service through the alleged deception. The relevant inquiry extended beyond whether the server handed Barton papers in the right place. It included why Barton had entered that place and what representations induced him to do so. The procedural posture matters: the ruling allowed the fraud issue to be adjudicated; it did not finally establish that every alleged representation had occurred.

learning.why: A plea alleging that deception induced an out-of-state defendant to enter the forum stated a basis for challenging service.

topics.cp-service: A formally delivered summons may still be challenged when fraud procured the defendant’s presence.
topics.cp-fraud-service: The court accepted the pleaded account of a deceptive invitation for purposes of testing the plea.
topics.cp-procedure-merits: Overruling a demurrer to an abatement plea permits factual adjudication; it does not establish that fraud actually occurred.
topics.cp-tag-jurisdiction: The service Barton attacked was personal service while physically present in West Virginia; the case is the fraud exception to transient (tag) jurisdiction.

learning.separateOpinions: The dissent read the circumstances differently, emphasizing that a real banquet existed and questioning whether the lawyer’s conduct amounted to the fraud necessary to invalidate service.

mnemonic.rationale: Lured across the state line by a phone call
